elements.id-string-3: We propose and analyze  an epidemiological model for vector borne diseases that integrates a multi-stage vector population and several host sub-populations which may be characterized by a variety of compartmental model types: subpopulations all include Susceptible and Infected compartments, but may or may not include Exposed and/or Recovered compartments.
elements.id-string-4: The model was originally designed  to evaluate the effectiveness of various prophylactic measures in malaria-endemic areas, but can be applied as well to other vector-borne diseases.
elements.id-string-5: This model is expressed as a system of several differential equations, where the number of equations depends on the particular assumptions of the model.
elements.id-string-6: We compute the basic reproduction number $\mathcal R_0$,and show  that if $\mathcal R_0\leqslant 1$, the disease free equilibrium (DFE)  is globally asymptotically stable (GAS) on the nonnegative orthant.If $\mathcal R_0>1$,  the system admits a unique endemic equilibrium (EE) that is GAS.
elements.id-string-7: We analyze the sensitivity of $R_0$ and the EE to different system parameters, and based on this analysis  we discuss the relative effectiveness  of different control measures.
elements.id-string-8: {\em Keywords:} Epidemiological model, Vector-borne, Basic reproduction number, Lyapunov function, Global asymptotic stability, Nonstandard finite difference scheme (NFDS), Simulation, Sensitivity, SEIRS
elements.id-string-11: Vector-borne infectious diseases such as malaria are widely spread in tropical regions, including parts of America, Asia and much of Africa.
elements.id-string-12: For example, infected mosquitoes serve as vectors for a number of serious and potentially fatal diseases, including malaria, yellow fever, Zika, and dengue fever.
elements.id-string-13: The mosquito life cycle includes multiple stages of questing and resting:  infections are transmitted when a mosquito that has bitten an infected host during a previous questing stage later bites an uninfected host during a subsequent questing stage.
elements.id-string-14: The chain of transmission for mosquito-borne diseases can be broken through the use of indoor or outdoor spraying, bed nets (which may be treated with insecticide) and prophylactic drugs, as well as other control strategies.
elements.id-string-15: Within the host population, individuals may be categorized into sub-populations based on the control measure(s) they use.
elements.id-string-16: A previous paper of Kamgang et {\em al.}~\cite{jck-19} represents a system with host sub-populations and vectors under the assumption that the host sub-populations can all be described with a SIS model.
elements.id-string-17: This model is itself an enhancement of several previous models~\cite{Macdonald78, Chit_08, Ross1911, NgwaMCM00, Zongo09}.
elements.id-string-18: These assumptions may be justified in cases where vector density is high, and there is rapid detection and treatment of infectious host individuals.
elements.id-string-19: However, in many important situations these assumptions are not applicable.
elements.id-string-20: For example, many endemic areas for vector-borne diseases are in poor sub-Saharan countries with very low revenue and poor medical structures, so disease go untreated.
elements.id-string-21: Moreover, in sub Saharan regions, the climate permits mosquito breeding year-round, and infections may still occur during periods of low vector density.
elements.id-string-22: Furthermore, people may develop immunity against malaria infection~\cite{AlOdAl, BarKris}.
elements.id-string-23: For these reasons,  it is more realistic to include Exposed(E) and Resistant/recovered(R) compartments of hosts, so that various sub-populations may obey SEIS, SIRS, or SEIRS models.

elements.id-string-39: In the following subsections, we provide a detailed description of the population structure and dynamics of hosts and vectors.
elements.id-string-41: The host population $H(t)$ is classified into $n$ subpopulations, indexed by $1,~2,~ \cdots,~ n$, depending on the way individuals in each subpopulation are disposed with respect to the infection.
elements.id-string-42: Individuals' disposition may depend on several factors, including protective measures employed; level of resistance to the disease; host species (if more than one species can serve as host); and so on.
elements.id-string-43: At time $t$,we let $H_i(t)~(i=1,~\,\cdots,~\,n)$ denote the size of the $i^{th}$ sub-population, so that $H(t) = {\dsum_{i=1}^n} H_i(t)$.

elements.id-string-52: The population of disease vectors is characterized by several classes, where each vector's class membership is determined by its own history of past and present activity.
elements.id-string-53: Before becoming infectious, vectors initially enter the Susceptible class: the rate of entry (that is, the recruitment rate) is $\Gamma$.
elements.id-string-54: Vectors alternate between two activities: {\it questing} (during which time the vectors interact with hosts, e.g. to bite for a blood meal) and {\it resting} (e.g. to lay down eggs, or to digest a blood meal).

elements.id-string-58: During an interaction involving an individual in the $i^{th}$ group, the  vector is killed with probability $\kappa_i$, while the probability the interaction is successful (i.e. the vector enters the resting state) is $\phi_i$ (so $\kappa_i + \phi_i \leqslant 1$).
elements.id-string-59: Following a successful interaction, the vector moves to the resting state.
elements.id-string-60: Letting $a$ denote the average number of interactions per vector per unit time (the {\em entomological  inoculation rate}), it follows that  at any given instant $t$, the incidence rate of successful interactions is $\varpiVar (t) \equiv \dsum_{i=1}^nah_i(t)\phi_i$,

elements.id-string-62: The infection rate for vectors may be computed as follows.
elements.id-string-63: Let $I_i, \xi_i$ denote the number of infectious hosts in group $i$ and the corresponding probability of vector infection per interaction with one of these hosts.
elements.id-string-64: Similarly, let $R_i,\widetilde\xi_i$ denote  the number of resistant hosts in group $i$ (when $v_i = 1$) and the corresponding per-interaction vector infection probability.

elements.id-string-66: Susceptible questing vectors that become infected enter the first Exposed resting class ($\mathrm{E}_r^{(\text 1)}$), while those which have not experienced successful infection stay uninfected and enter the Susceptible resting class ($\mathrm{S}_r$).
elements.id-string-67: Following initial infection, the vector must remain alive for a certain period before becoming Infectious (this period is called the {\em extrinsic incubation period} in the biological and medical literature ~\cite{010047862}).
elements.id-string-68: During this period, the vector experiences a positive number of resting/questing cycles.
elements.id-string-69: In our model, we suppose that a vector becomes infectious after a fixed number $\ell$ of resting/questing cycles following initial infection.
elements.id-string-70: These successive resting/questing cycles are modeled as a sequence of $2\ell$ Exposed states, and are denoted by $ \mathrm{E}^{(\text 1)}_q,\mathrm{E}^{(\text 2)}_r, \cdots, \mathrm{E}^{(\ell)}_q,\mathrm{E}^{(\ell+1)}_r$.
elements.id-string-71: If a vector survives through all of these states, it then enters the Infectious class, which is further divided into questing and resting sub-classes ($\mathrm{I}_q$ and $\mathrm{I}_r$, respectively).
elements.id-string-72: Once a vector enters the Infectious class, it remains there for the rest of its life, alternating between resting and questing states.
